pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A courier makes money on stops that are delivered the first time. This workspace keeps every delivery, route and client in one place so dispatch can see the day, drivers know their order, and the owner can see which clients and routes pay.
Pickup to proof
Deliveries

: one row per pickup-and-drop. It moves Booked, Assigned, Picked up, Out for delivery, then Delivered, or Failed attempt with a reason. After three failed attempts it is Returned to sender. Mark delivered stamps the day; Log failed attempt keeps it open for a retry.
Clients
: pharmacies, law firms, labs, parts stores, florists and online shops that send with you, their billing and pickup notes, with delivered and failed counts and a First-attempt rate.
Routes
: each driver's run for a day, with vehicle, miles and fuel. Stops, delivered stops, revenue and driver pay roll up; Route margin appears when the route is closed out.
Claims
: damaged, lost or late deliveries a client wants paid for.
The dispatch day
7:00: dispatch opens Deliveries, This week view, and assigns every Booked stop for today to a route and driver.
Order stops: rush and specimen stops first, cold chain before warm, legal filings before the clerk closes.
Drivers press Mark delivered at the door with a signature or a door photo.
Failed attempt: the driver picks the reason and leaves a note; the client is texted within 15 minutes.
3:00: dispatch works Failed attempts to re-plan and puts each retry on the next route.
At check-in, the driver enters miles and fuel and dispatch presses Close out route.
Dispatcher, drivers, account desk
Proof that holds up
A signature, or a photo that shows the parcel and the door number, and the time. Without one, a claim is ours to pay.
Failed attempts to re-plan
Not yet on a driver
Open claims

text.text: A failed attempt costs a second trip and often a client. Most are preventable before the van leaves. This page is how the team keeps the first-attempt rate above 95 percent and what to do when a drop fails anyway.
Before the route
Check every new address against the client's note; online shop orders are the most likely to be wrong.
Businesses: confirm closing time. A dental office that closes at 4 cannot take a 4:30 drop.
Homes: if the client allows it, text the recipient the window the night before.
Medical and legal items are signature only; never plan them as leave-at-door.
At the door
Knock and wait one full minute. Call the number on the ticket.
Safe place allowed and the item is not signature-only: leave it, take the photo with the door number in frame.
Otherwise press Log failed attempt and choose the reason: Nobody home, Business closed, Wrong address, Refused, No safe place.
Leave a card with the dispatch number and the next window.
Re-planning

cells.text: Retry on the next route, text the new window
Retry first thing the next business day
Call the client for the correct one before any retry
Return to sender the same day; tell the client why
Ask the recipient for a neighbour or pickup point

text.text: After three failed attempts the delivery is Returned to sender, and the client is billed for the attempts under their rate card.
Reading the rate
Each client shows a First-attempt rate. Under 90 percent means a conversation: a cut-off time, better addresses, or a different service.
Checklist at 3 pm
Every failed attempt has a reason and a photo
Every retry is on a route with a window
Clients texted about each failed drop
A route is the unit you pay drivers and fuel on, so it is where margin is won or lost. This page covers how dispatch builds a route in the morning and how a driver closes it out in the evening.
Building it
Create the route for the date, pick the driver and vehicle. A cargo e-bike suits downtown legal runs; a van suits pharmacy totes.
Assign each delivery to the route. Group by area, then by deadline.
Rush and specimen stops go first; cold items ride in coolers and are delivered within 90 minutes of pickup.
Move the route to Loaded once everything is scanned on board, and On the road when the driver leaves.
During the day
New same-day bookings go to the route nearest the pickup, not the emptiest one, and the driver is told by text before the next stop.
Dispatch watches Out for delivery; a stop not moving for 45 minutes gets a call.
Closing out
The driver checks in and every stop is Delivered or Failed attempt with a reason.
Undelivered items go back on the shelf with a tag; nothing stays in the van overnight.
Enter Miles driven and Fuel and tolls.
Press Close out route. Route margin appears: delivered revenue less driver pay and fuel.
Reading route margin

cells.text: Too many miles or too many failed stops; redraw the area

text.text: Worked example

The east side route ran three stops: two delivered for 76 in revenue, and 47 paid to the driver, because the failed bouquet drop is still paid. With 9 in fuel, close out shows a 20 margin, well under 35 percent, so the florist retry goes on the denser midday route instead of its own trip.
The dispatcher's screen from 6 am: every stop by where it is in the day, the routes on the road, and the rush jobs still without a driver.

pages.title: Taking and sending a rush job

text.text: A rush job is a two-hour promise made on the phone. Most of the time it is won or lost in the first ten minutes: the questions you ask, and which driver you send.
On the call
Pickup and drop addresses, a name and phone at both ends, and the business hours of the drop.
What it is: pieces, weight, and anything special (a lab specimen on ice, signed legal papers, a part that will not fit a car).
The deadline, as a time, not as as soon as possible.
Price it before you hang up: rush is the standard rate plus the rush fee, and the client hears the total.
Who to send

cells.text: The e-bike or the closest car
Across town, under an hour of driving
The driver whose next stop is nearest the pickup, if their route can absorb 40 minutes
A van; never promise a van you do not have
A driver who has done that client before

text.text: While it runs
Book the stop as Rush, 2 hours with the window set to the promised time. It shows on the Rush and same day list until delivered.
Text the client the driver's name at pickup and the photo at delivery.
If the driver will be late, call the client before the window passes, never after.
When you cannot do it
Say so on the call. A declined rush keeps a client; a missed one loses them. Offer the earliest time you can keep, or a scheduled next-morning slot at the normal price.
At the end of the day
Every rush delivered with signature or door photo
Rush fee on the stop's price
Any late rush written up on the client's page with the reason
